Middletown.wildlife_intro:
Middletown keeps our crew busy with Norway rats downtown, raccoons and squirrels in the older housing, and groundhogs and skunks at the farm edges. Wallkill River valley  gives wildlife food, water, and cover within a short run of almost every roof in town, and the housing does the rest — once an animal finds a soft soffit, an uncapped chimney, or a gap at the roofline, it treats the house as part of its territory.

The year has a rhythm in Middletown. Fall pushes squirrels, raccoons, and rodents indoors ahead of winter; spring brings denning mothers looking for chimneys and attic corners; summer is when bat colonies are most visible in older homes and when young animals start ranging on their own. Most Middletown jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

Port Jervis.wildlife_intro:
Port Jervis sits where the Neversink meets the Delaware at the tri-state corner, a rail-and-river city of Victorian homes climbing steep streets above the confluence. Raccoons work the hillside attics and chimneys, Norway rats hold the oldest downtown and riverfront blocks, and the wooded bluffs behind the city keep skunks and opossums in the yards year-round. The rivers give the city mild winters by upstate standards — and a longer active season for everything.

Steep lots define the inspections here: retaining walls, stacked porches, and roofs at three levels on one house. High water on the Delaware pushes rats and ground-level animals uphill into foundations, a pattern Port Jervis homeowners know well. Our crew inspects from the cellar up, removes the animals, and seals both levels, because in a river city the foundation entries matter as much as the roofline.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Warwick?
faqs.a: Warwick quotes depend on whether the job is a village house or a farm property with barns and sheds in scope. We inspect the structures you want covered, show you the burrows and entries, and give you a written figure for removal and screening.

faqs.q: Why are groundhogs so destructive around Warwick farms?
faqs.a: The valley's deep, soft soils — including the famous black dirt — are easy digging, and a groundhog family can undermine a barn foundation or shed floor in one season. Removing the animals without screening the structure leaves the burrow system vacant for the next tenant; our crew does both, and checks field-edge burrows near buildings as part of the inspection.

Warwick.wildlife_intro:
Warwick is Orange County's farm valley town: a historic village, the hamlets of Florida and Pine Island in the black-dirt onion country, Greenwood Lake to the south, and orchards and pastures in every direction. Groundhogs are the headline animal — the valley's fields, stone walls, and barn foundations are excavated every spring — with skunks around the farmsteads and raccoons and bats in the village's older homes.

Black-dirt country changes the burrowing math: rich, soft soil lets groundhogs build systems fast, and burrows migrate from field edges to under barns within a season. Our crew treats Warwick properties as farm properties — house inspection plus outbuilding screening — removes the animals, and seals the dwelling. Village homes get the same attic-and-chimney attention, with the valley's heavy skunk population checked under every porch.

Monroe.wildlife_intro:
Monroe, in Orange County's southeast, is commuter suburbia wrapped around lakes and state-park woods — the village, the town's subdivisions, and Mombasha and Walton lakes in the hills. Squirrels and raccoons generate most calls from the postwar and newer neighborhoods, while the lake properties add raccoons under low decks and bats in cottage eaves. Harriman State Park's forest presses directly against the town's western and northern edges, keeping animal pressure high on every street that backs onto woods.

Park-edge living sets the Monroe pattern: a subdivision can be thoroughly suburban in front and forest at the back fence, and animals use the back. Our crew inspects Monroe homes with the lot's edge in mind, removes the animals, and seals the house — then screens the deck and shed voids on the wooded lots, where most repeat Monroe complaints actually originate.

faqs.q: Are bats common in Goshen's older homes?
faqs.a: Very — big brown bats have used Goshen's pre-war eaves and attics for generations, and the surrounding farmland feeds them well. Removal is exclusion only: one-way exits installed and every other gap sealed, timed around the maternity season as professional practice so young bats are not sealed inside. Our crew finds the entries at inspection, including the secondary gaps a big roof always has.

Goshen.wildlife_intro:
Goshen is Orange County's seat, a handsome historic village of church spires and the Historic Track, surrounded by some of the county's best farm country. Bats are the village call that defines it — the 1800s homes and big church-adjacent houses offer eave and attic space in abundance — while the surrounding farms produce groundhogs along the fields, skunks under barns, and raccoons everywhere. The black-dirt fields begin just south of the village.

Historic-village rules apply in Goshen: the inspection has to respect old trim and older chimneys, and entries hide behind both. Summer colonies announce themselves by staining and odor at one eave; the rest of the roofline usually has more. Our crew inspects Goshen homes fully, removes the animals, and seals with the house's age in mind — and on the farm properties, screens the barn and shed voids in the same visit.
